Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

19 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the sailboat, right of center Light: the setting sun, low on the horizon just left of center, behind the scene and to the boat's leftHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: Paint the far hill and shoreFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 3/4 inch flat: Cover the water in tealFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat (on its edge): Dash in the path in dull goldFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • small round: Break the path with teal ripplesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • liner: Line in the mast and boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The sails. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 3.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 4.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 7.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 10.
  • Liner work, first in step 12. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Pull-down, first in step 16.
  • Zigzag, first in step 18.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sunset sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 19 · The sunset sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area: from the top edge down to a little past where the water will start, about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and all the way across.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Sky violet, Coral pink, then Sunset orange.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with Sky violet at the top and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up Coral pink and paint below it, then Sunset orange below that. Then stroke back up over each join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: The light comes from the sun, low on the horizon just left of the middle, so the sky is brightest and most orange around it and the boat will be lit from its left. Carry the orange a little below where the water will start; the hill and the water go over it later. While it's still wet, drag a few loose level streaks of violet and coral into the bands so they aren't clean stripes.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 19 · The sunset sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 3/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. With the tip of the brush, make small circular strokes that move outward from the middle of the sun until the disc is the size the Where picture shows.
  7. It should leave a round disc with a slightly soft edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is ragged. Fix: go around it again with the same small circular motion, in lighter passes.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is about the size of a large coin. Start with a dot in its middle and circle outward until it's round; keep the edge clean against the orange sky.

Small circles

Not checked yet

Motion. Small circles with the tip of the brush make a cloud's bumpy top edge. Around a sun or moon, circular strokes move outward from it.

What it leaves. A bumpy, soft edge.

Then. Smooth with the same circular motion, and highlight only the lit top edges.

Little circles along the top

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • The edge is too hard. Soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

The far shore 1 step

STEP 3 OF 19 · The far shore, 1 of 1

Paint the far hill and shore

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  4. Paint: Hill purple.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Bend every stroke with the shape: follow the hump of the hill over its top and down its long right slope, then run level strokes along the shore.
  7. It should leave marks that bend with the hill, which is what makes it look sloped, and a level dark band for the shore.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The hill is one low hump on the left, highest about 2 in from the left edge, sloping down to the right until it thins into the shore just under the sun. Carry the shore line straight on to the right edge, right through where the sails will be. Keep it flat and soft: it's far away, so it gets no texture.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

The water 3 steps

STEP 4 OF 19 · The water, 1 of 3

Cover the water in teal

  1. Let the far shore and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Teal water.
  4. Mix enough Teal water for this step and steps 5 and 9; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  6. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  7. It should leave flat, level bands that read as ground or water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: Paint right through where the sun's path, the boat and its reflection will go; they are painted on top once this is dry. Keep the top edge level and tight against the purple shore.

STEP 5 OF 19 · The water, 2 of 3

Streak the deep teal

  1. Let the water and the far shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Teal water.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right, lifting off at the end of each so the streaks have broken ends.
  6. It should leave level streaks of deeper teal that read as water stretching away: fewer and thinner toward the back, darker and closer together in front.
  7. Leave what step 4 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: Use the same Teal water, laid on a little thicker, with a touch more ultramarine worked into it for the deepest streaks along the bottom edge and in the two bottom corners. Keep the streaks long and level, and leave gaps of the flat coat between them, more gaps toward the shore.

The sun's path 3 steps

STEP 7 OF 19 · The sun's path, 1 of 3

Dash in the path in dull gold

  1. Let the water and the far shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 1/2 in wide and 4 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dull gold.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat (on its edge). Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  5. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  6. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the water color between them.
  7. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.

Tip: The path starts as a narrow band right under the sun at the shore and gets wider and more broken toward the bottom of the canvas. Put a few stray dashes out to the left, about halfway down the water. This dull gold is the soft outer layer; the bright orange goes over its middle next.

Brighten the path with orange

STEP 9 OF 19 · The sun's path, 3 of 3

Break the path with teal ripples

  1. Let the sun's path on the water and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 1/2 in wide and 4 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Teal water.
  5. Brush: small round. Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  6. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  7. It should leave short, flat, level teal marks that split the path into bars, wider apart lower down.
  8. Leave what steps 7 and 8 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  9. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Pull each teal dash across the path from its edge toward the middle, so the gold and orange end up as separate level bars with water between them. Use more gaps lower down, where the path is widest.

The sailboat 6 steps

STEP 10 OF 19 · The sailboat, 1 of 6

Block in the two sails

  1. Let the water and the far shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 1/4 in from the right edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
  5. Paint: Sail cream.
  6. Mix enough Sail cream for this step and steps 11 and 19; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Start with one simple shape: the taller right triangle, with its upright side where the mast will go. Then add the second piece, the left triangle, leaning against the other side of the mast line.
  9. It should leave two flat cream triangles with a narrow gap or overlap between them where the mast will go.

Tip: The sails are two tall triangles side by side with a thin gap for the mast: the right one is taller and its point is the top of the boat; the left one starts a little lower and leans left. Together they are about as wide at the foot as two thirds of their height. Their feet sit level, a little below the shore line.

STEP 11 OF 19 · The sailboat, 2 of 6

Brush light and shadow into the sails

  1. Let the sails and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.

STEP 12 OF 19 · The sailboat, 3 of 6

Line in the mast and boom

  1. Let the sails and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 1/4 in from the right edge; it's about 1 3/4 in wide and 4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Mast brown.
  5. Mix enough Mast brown for this step and step 18; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull the mast from the top down in one go, then the boom from the mast out to the right.
  8. It should leave two thin, straight, dark lines: an upright mast and a shorter level boom.
  9. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: Pull the mast in one line from just above the sails' top point straight down to the water, between the two triangles. The boom runs level along the foot of the right sail. To thicken a line, go over it once more rather than pressing harder.

Pull down the hull's dark reflection

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A small red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with its reflection, the low sun and its orange light path, and a purple hill on the far shore.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is a painting-style picture edge to edge: no bars, text, border, or watermark.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 11 x 14 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: the left 7.5% (the far left end of the purple hill) and the right 7.5% (empty sky and water right of the boat)

Why: The picture is 3:2 and the canvas is 14:11, so about 7.5% comes off each side. The boat, its reflection, the sun and the sun path all stay whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: none but the boat, which is the subject. Textures of hundreds of items: no, the water is loose level streaks. Detail inside big shapes: no. More parts than the budget of 8: no.

Changed: nothing

Why: Every answer is no, so the lesson is made from the photo as fitted to the canvas.

A calm sunset: a sky that fades from violet through coral to orange, a teal sea, and one small red boat with white sails and its long rippled reflection. The sky and water are easy and big; what's hard is the small boat (two clean triangles, a straight mast, a low hull) and keeping the reflection softer than the boat. The lesson is mostly about water: a flat coat, streaks, a sun path in dashes, and a reflection built in order.

Subject: A red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset
Focal point: the sailboat, right of center
Light: the setting sun, low on the horizon just left of center, behind the scene and to the boat's left

What it saw, back to front

  1. The sunset sky
  2. The far hill and shore
  3. The water
  4. The sails
  5. The mast and boom
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A sunset over water with one boat is a classic paint-along subject: a blended sky first, a far hill, the water, then the boat and its reflection on top. The owner's pick for beginner acrylic is paint-along on a white canvas (docs/decisions.md), and its water-reflection rules fit this picture directly.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It starts with a toned ground and a flat block-in of everything, then refines. This picture is mostly two blended gradients (sky, water) that are easier painted once, wet, straight on white; a burnt sienna tone would dull the teal water.

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Sky violet Delta E 4.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part red

  • Coral pink Delta E 2.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part red, 1 part white, a touch of ultramarine

  • Sunset orange Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

  • Sun yellow Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

  • Hill purple Delta E 2.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white

  • Teal water Delta E 9.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

  • Soft gray-teal Delta E 2.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow

  • Dull gold Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

  • Path orange Delta E 2.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part yellow, 1 part red, 1 part white, a touch of ultramarine

  • Sail cream Delta E 3.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

  • Boat red Delta E 4.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of white

  • Deck tan Delta E 2.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow

  • Mast brown Delta E 2.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, 1 part white

Furthest off: Delta E 9.8. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order19 steps

Back to front, as the technique says: the sky first, carried past the horizon; the sun on it; the far hill and shore over it; then the water as a flat coat and two streak passes. The sun's path goes on the dry water in two layers (dull gold, then a smaller orange) and is broken with teal ripples. Then the boat, also back to front: sails, the mast over them, the hull in front of the mast's foot. The reflection comes last, after everything above the water is dry, in the research's order: colors pulled down, the mast's zigzag, then level cream dashes across.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The sky is behind everything and is one wet blend, so it goes first and all in one step.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    A small disc on the dry sky; it sets the light for every highlight after it.

  3. 3. Paint the far hill and shore

    The farthest land, flat and soft, painted over the sky before the water meets it.

  4. 4. Cover the water in teal

    One flat coat of teal gives the water its edge and something to streak over; it runs under the boat.

  5. 5. Streak the deep teal

    The deeper streaks first, darkest before lighter, so the texture builds in passes instead of appearing at once (check failed the single streak step at 16% of the picture).

  6. 6. Streak the lighter gray-teal

    The lighter streaks over the deep ones finish the water before anything sits on it.

  7. 7. Dash in the path in dull gold

    The sun path's first, wider, duller layer, on dry water.

  8. 8. Brighten the path with orange

    The second layer, brighter and smaller, as the research says a sun path is built.

  9. 9. Break the path with teal ripples

    Teal dashes cut the path into bars so it reads as light on moving water.

  10. 10. Block in the two sails

    The boat starts with its biggest shape, the sails, as two flat triangles over the dry sky and shore.

  11. 11. Brush light and shadow into the sails

    Light and shadow on the sails once their shape is right.

  12. 12. Line in the mast and boom

    The mast and boom are thin dark lines over the dry sails.

  13. 13. Block in the red hull

    The hull sits in front of the mast's foot, so it's blocked in after the mast.

  14. 14. Line the deck in cream

    The pale deck line along the hull's top, a liner line on the dry red.

  15. 15. Round the hull with darker and brighter red

    Brighter and darker red round the hull; it's the hull's last step and shows it finished.

  16. 16. Pull down the hull's dark reflection

    Reflections start once the boat is dry: the hull's red, pulled down right under it.

  17. 17. Pull down the sails' gray-teal reflection

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • outline refuses a plan with no stages ('the plan has no stages with steps'), though skill step 2 says to outline with stages still empty. Worked around with one placeholder step and paint per part, then cleared them before `paints` so it would measure with no steps (a placeholder step naming one paint makes `paints` give each part exactly one color, a single pink for the whole sky).
  • The sliver of water between the sails' foot and the hull, and a thin rim around the hull, were claimed by no part, so the outline tool gave them to the sky (the backdrop), and build-steps drew a gray boat-shaped blob there from step 1. Two rounds on the sails' boxes did nothing; what fixed it was points_in on the water part (an area), placed on the gap and on the hull, so the water's outline runs under the boat. The skill's table lists points only for marks and thin parts.
  • paints measured the water as one teal (#3a768f) though the finish has a darker teal at the bottom and lighter streaks; the lighter and darker water is taught as the same paint with a touch of white or blue, not as a new mix.
  • On the second paints run (after the steps were written) the mast's brown and the dark of the reflection measured as one paint (Mast brown, 3.7 apart), and the hull's reflection merged into Boat red (5.9 apart). So the reflection is taught with the boat's own paints; the technique's rule that a reflection is never the exact same mix is kept in the text as a tip (dull the red with a touch of Mast brown), not as a separate measured paint.
  • Adding a part after paints exist is refused by outline until some paint lists the new part in its `parts`, but paints (which writes that list) needs outline first. Worked around by adding the part to one paint's `parts` by hand before outline, then running paints again.
  • Card lines rewritten for this subject: small-circles (cloud wording on a sun: motion, result, watch-out); curved-strokes (pumpkin and balloon wording, on the hill, the sails and the hull); build-from-pieces (oval and ( ) pieces, on two triangular sails and a hull); liner (branch wording, on a mast and a deck line); horizontal-dashes ('near the horizon' on a reflection under a hull); pull-down ('tree, boat, or shore' result; where to start); horizontal-strokes (result line for streak passes); side-to-side-blend (colors named in order).
  • Not in the cards or research: how to paint straight triangular sails and a straight mast. build-from-pieces and liner were the closest cards; a card for straight-edged shapes (a flat brush's edge pulled along a line) is missing.
  • The tips for the water's lighter and darker streaks, the sails' shadow, and the hull's light and dark red tell the painter to shift the step's own paint with a touch of white or a darker paint; that follows the lighter-darker basics card, not a measured paint.
  • The fresh-context text review (skill step 7b) could not be run: this run had no Agent tool. The author looked at three review sheets instead and said so in review.json.
  • Teal water turned unreachable (Delta E 9.8) once the water was measured as two paints; the five tubes can't make a teal that saturated.
